opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that I don't see them as two separate things to balance. A lot of people frame it as a seesaw: on one side you have the curiosity-driven, long-horizon research, and on the other you have the product, the thing that has to ship and make money. But I think the most interesting research questions right now actually come from trying to make something real.

Take my own background. For years I worked on visual representation learning, on architectures, on self-supervised learning. Many of the questions we studied looked very academic at the time. But they mattered because, eventually, someone has to build a system that sees and understands the world. When you try to build that system, you discover that the problems you assumed were solved are not solved at all. Building is a very good way of being honest with yourself about what you don't know.

So in the lab, I want the research agenda to be shaped by a real goal, something ambitious and concrete, rather than by what will get accepted at the next conference. At the same time, I don't want to be pulled into short-term product iterations. That's the trap: you become a company that fine-tunes and wraps things, and you stop asking fundamental questions.

My practical rule is this. Keep a small number of very big bets, the ones you believe are scientifically right even if they take years. Then make sure every bet has a path to something tangible along the way, like a model, a system, or a capability people can touch. Those milestones are not distractions. They are checkpoints that tell you whether your scientific belief holds up.

Culture matters too. I want people who can read a paper deeply and then also go debug a data pipeline at two in the morning. In academia, those two kinds of people are often separate. In a lab like this, I think they have to be the same people, or at least work very closely together.

And frankly, a bit of stubbornness helps. The field moves fast, and there's huge pressure to follow whatever the current trend is, whether that's scaling the same recipe or chasing the same benchmarks. Being frontier means sometimes being out of consensus. But being real means you can't stay out of consensus forever without evidence. So you hold your conviction, and you let the things you build prove you right or wrong.

r001.rationale: The response discusses big research bets and tangible milestones, but gives no 20–30 percent allocation or proposal to reserve part of the lab for freely pursued frontier research.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest's response directly.

I think the honest answer is that I don't see them as two things to balance, and the moment you frame it as a trade-off, you've already lost something.

Let me explain what I mean. The best research I've ever been part of, going back to ResNeXt, to ConvNeXt, to the diffusion transformer work, none of it came from sitting in a room saying "let's do frontier research." It came from a very concrete problem. Somebody was trying to make something work, and the existing tools broke, and you had to understand why. The research question emerges from the friction of building. If you don't build, you don't feel the friction, and then you end up working on problems that are elegant but nobody actually has.

At the same time, if you only build, you become a product company that happens to use AI, and the frontier moves without you. In this field, the frontier moves so fast that if you're not generating some of that motion yourself, you're perpetually six months behind, integrating someone else's ideas. That's a fine business, but it's not a lab.

So what I want is a place where the loop is tight. Researchers should have to confront real users, real data, real failure modes. Not through a product manager's slide deck, but directly. And the people building the real thing should have permission, actually an expectation, to stop and ask the deep question when something doesn't make sense, instead of patching around it.

The failure mode I worry about most isn't picking the wrong ratio. It's the two groups drifting apart culturally. Research starts optimizing for papers and benchmarks, product starts optimizing for shipping dates, and they stop talking. Then you have two mediocre organizations under one name. I'd rather have a small team where everyone is slightly uncomfortable, where the researcher is embarrassed that their method doesn't work on real data, and the engineer is embarrassed that they don't understand why their system behaves the way it does. That discomfort is the signal that you're in the right place.

And honestly, coming from academia, part of why I'm doing this is that I've seen what you can't do with students and limited compute. Academia is great at asking questions, but it's increasingly hard to answer them without touching the real scale. A lab lets you close that gap. But only if "making something real" is treated as part of the research, not as the tax you pay to fund it.

r001.rationale: The response rejects framing research and building as a ratio to balance and proposes no 20–30 percent allocation for freely pursued frontier research.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make those two things reinforce each other. Frontier research needs room for uncertainty. If every project has to justify itself with a product milestone next quarter, you’re going to miss ideas that take longer to develop. But you also need to build something that people can actually use, because that exposes gaps you might never notice in a benchmark.

So I would give research a longer horizon, while keeping a very short feedback loop with building. When we put a model into a real workflow, where does it fail? Is that an engineering problem, or does it reveal a capability we fundamentally don’t have yet? That distinction should help shape the research agenda.

The balance isn’t necessarily fifty-fifty. It’s having a clear connection between the scientific questions we pursue and the things we want to make possible, without pretending we already know the path between them.

r001.rationale: The response supports giving research a longer horizon, but it does not propose reserving roughly 20–30 percent of the lab for freely pursued frontier research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important thing is to make those two things reinforce each other. Frontier research gives you the possibility of building something fundamentally different. But when you try to make it work for someone, you discover constraints that your benchmark didn’t capture. Those constraints can become very good research questions.

For the lab, I would want a clear long-term research direction, with enough room for people to pursue ideas that might not work immediately. At the same time, we should have something concrete that forces us to test our assumptions. Can people actually use it? Is it reliable? Does it solve a problem they care about?

The balance doesn’t have to be fifty-fifty every week. Sometimes you need to step back and explore; sometimes you need to focus and make the thing work. What matters is that the research and the building stay connected, and that we learn from both.

r001.rationale: The response supports allowing time for exploratory research, but it does not propose reserving roughly 20–30 percent of the lab for it.
